A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. It usually grows on basic soils at scrub edges and occurs less often on rocks and fixed coastal dunes.
A perennial, rhizome-growing plant native to the Allegheny and Cherokee mountains of the east-central United States, where it grows in the temperate biome.
A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. It grows at the edges or beneath deciduous woodland and scrub, favouring shady, acidic soils rich in organic matter.

A rhizomatous perennial whose two listed subspecies are native to mainland Portugal. It has narrow, usually undivided leaves and yellow or pale-yellow flowers. Subspecies aquatilis inhabits freshwater wetlands and rice fields, while subspecies maritimus grows in estuaries, salt marshes and coastal lagoons on wet, salty soils.

A plant considered indigenous in Switzerland, with a wider distribution that may be southern European. It grows on Picris hieracioides and is distinguished by stamens densely hairy below but nearly bare or only slightly glandular above.
A subtropical subshrub native to the western Mediterranean, southern Greece and Lebanon.

A flowering herb native to mainland Portugal. It has pale pink flowers and unequal calyx teeth fringed along their length with long hairs, and it grows mainly in sandy meadows, pastures and open woodland.
A shrub or tree hybrid native to northern China. It is a cross between Juniperus chinensis and J. sabina and grows mainly in temperate regions.
An epiphytic subshrub native from eastern Nepal to Indo-China. It grows mainly in seasonally dry tropical regions.

A flowering plant native to Ecuador, Peru and Bolivia. Its leaves yield a fibre called fique, used to make ropes and various woven goods; the flower stalk is also used for structures such as ladders, posts and huts.
A spreading succulent native to South Africa's southwestern Cape Provinces. It grows in sandy places.
A geophyte whose native origin is not supplied. In Portugal it grows in shaded, generally acidic ground within or around cork-oak woods, holm-oak woods, pinewoods and scrub.

An annual flowering plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula. It inhabits sparse mountain grasslands on rocky or gravelly ground; in Portugal it occurs in the mountains of Trás-os-Montes and Beira Interior.
A plant presumed to originate in South America. It is naturalised in Portugal in wet meadows, beside waterways and in landscaped urban spaces, and is legally classed as invasive in Madeira.

A genus of algae whose native origin is not supplied. Its cells are typically spherical but may become angularly flattened, forming irregular packets or layered clusters during division; in older cells, the chloroplast partly detaches from the cell wall.
Annual grass endemic to the Iberian Peninsula. In Portugal it grows in mountain fields, fallow ground and pastures, especially on dry, acidic, sandy soils derived from granite.
Shrub native from central Portugal to west-central Spain, growing mainly in the temperate biome.
Flowering plant native to Peru, northwestern Argentina and central Chile. An early account recorded it beside rivers near Concepción, Chile.

Low-growing, solitary rosette-forming aloe found mainly from northwestern Eswatini through Mpumalanga to Limpopo, South Africa. Its dark-lined green leaves have prominent reddish-brown toothed edges, while its branched flower stalks bear dull brick-red to coral-red flowers.
Bulb-growing plant native to southeastern France and the central and southern Iberian Peninsula, occurring mainly in the temperate biome.
Plant tribe found worldwide in coastal and inland salty ground. Its members typically have fleshy stems that appear jointed, greatly reduced leaves and dense, thick, spike-like flower clusters.

Annual flowering plant with no native origin given in the supplied sources. In Portugal it grows mainly on trampled urban or rural ground, including paths and gaps between paving stones, and less often in temporary natural meadows beside paths.
Subshrub native to South Africa's Cape Province, growing mainly in the subtropical biome.
Semi-succulent annual or subshrub native to the southwestern and southern Cape Province of South Africa. It grows mainly in the subtropical biome.
Shrub native to the southwestern Cape Province of South Africa, growing mainly in the subtropical biome.
A flowering plant endemic to South Africa’s Cape Provinces. Its growth habit is notably stemless.
A woody climbing vine native from the Himalayas through central and southern China and northern Indochina to Taiwan. It grows mainly in temperate regions.
A genus of evergreen flowering succulents. Its members have long, grooved leaves and flower heads without the petal-like outer florets typical of daisies.
A succulent native to parts of South Africa’s Eastern Cape. It forms a compact cushion of sprawling stems with smooth, angular leaves that are triangular in cross-section.
A perennial native to southwestern Portugal. It grows mainly in the subtropical biome.

A perennial herb native from Eritrea to southern Africa, Madagascar and nearby Indian Ocean islands, and the Arabian Peninsula. Its slender stems twine or trail, bearing heart-shaped to arrow-shaped leaves and small pinkish, pale purple or white flowers.
An evergreen, spiny succulent shrub endemic to South Africa’s southern Cape Province. It has thick, segmented blue-green branches and spreads underground to form extensive dense stands.
A succulent subshrub native to the Northern Province. It grows mainly in desert or dry shrubland.
An aquatic flowering herb of lowland wetlands. It may grow above the water or drift submerged; the supplied sources disagree about its native origin.
An annual grass, it grows in Portugal in annual grasslands on poor, sandy or stony soils.

A perennial succulent native to Namibia, South Africa and Lesotho, with an isolated Namibian population in the Auas Mountains. It forms low mats of upright or creeping stems, with persistent reddish-green leaves and white to cream tubular flowers.
An annual grass, it grows in wet or waterlogged meadows in Portugal.

A shrub or small tree native to South Africa, it grows in moist, partly shaded forest and along forest margins. It has small, often shallowly lobed heart-shaped leaves and clusters of sweetly scented white flowers.
A perennial sedge native to Cape Province. It grows mainly in the subtropical biome.
A succulent endemic to South Africa's Western Cape, it forms part of the fynbos vegetation.
A succulent endemic to South Africa's Western Cape, it forms part of the fynbos vegetation. Its range extends from Tulbagh to Worcester and the Langeberg.
A flowering plant recorded from Africa.
A moss recorded as common at numerous mountain and forest sites. Some records describe it growing on holm oak and cork oak trunks.
A perennial plant native to southwestern Cape Province. It grows mainly in the subtropical region.
A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal.
A vascular flowering plant found across Europe, including Ukraine, but absent from the central south and far north.
An annual herb found across most of southern and central Europe, Turkey and the Caucasus. Its hairy, branching stems bear rounded purple or pink flower heads, and the plant self-pollinates.
A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. It grows in cultivated fields, along roads and beside waterways, especially in disturbed places.
A subshrub or shrub native to a range extending from Taiwan to northern Borneo. It grows mainly in subtropical regions.

An alga whose native origin is not supplied, Dasycladus vermicularis contains three sulfated metabolites identified from its extracts. Two—sulfated benzoic and phenylacetic acids—were reported as previously unknown natural products.
An aquatic flowering plant native to mainland Portugal, thin-leaved horned-pondweed inhabits ponds and marshes. It grows in fresh or moderately brackish water.

A flowering plant endemic to mainland Portugal, Adenocarpus anisochilus occurs mainly in the south and southwest, with an isolated population near Sintra. It grows in scrub beside forests, cork-oak woods and waterways, favouring deep acidic soils, and readily colonises abandoned forestry and farmland.
A tree native from Vanuatu to New Caledonia, Ficus habrophylla grows primarily in wet tropical environments.

A moss whose native origin is not supplied, Alpine Thread-moss has been recorded at scattered sites in Algeria, including Blida, Constantine, Djurdjura and the Aurès Mountains. It is described as rare.

A shrub endemic to Macaronesia, Canary Hare's Ear occurs on Madeira, Porto Santo, El Hierro and La Gomera, with different varieties and subspecies having narrower ranges. It has narrow grey-green leaves and loose, elongated clusters of yellow flowers.

A herbaceous plant originating in the Canary Islands, Andryala glandulosa has leaves with wavy, curled edges and flower heads carried on long stalks. Its subspecies have differing distributions across the Canary Islands and Madeira.

A woody-based perennial or small shrub whose native origin is not supplied, Sonchus parathalassius has thick branching stems and fleshy, deeply divided leaves clustered at their tips. Its upright branched flower clusters bear numerous yellow flower heads.

A perennial herb whose native origin is not explicitly supplied, rough-leaved phlomis has a narrow Mediterranean distribution extending into Transcaucasia, Anatolia and the Maghreb. Its rough, opposite leaves accompany tiers of purple, two-lipped flowers, and it inhabits dry pastures, disturbed ground and slopes.
A climber native from southern China to Hainan and Taiwan, Bentham's Rosewood grows primarily in wet tropical environments.

A perennial liverwort of unstated native origin. Its blue-grey, fleshy, velvet-like body is heart-shaped, with fringed edges that curl upward in dry conditions. Thickened tips help it overwinter and reproduce without spores.

A section of 38 sedge species with no single native origin stated; its diversity is centred in Europe and adjoining parts of Africa and Asia. Members share short primary rhizomes, sheathing leaf-like bracts and three stigmas in female flowers. Its two subsections favour different soils, either acidic or basic to metal-rich.
A perennial herb of unstated native origin, reported from France, Spain and Portugal. It has a tuberous underground stem, yellow flower heads and hairy fruits topped with bristles or scales.

A small deciduous tree described as endemic to Spain’s Cantabrian range, with additional occurrences in the Iberian System near Teruel. Often stunted or shrubby, it has late-emerging leaves with uneven rounded lobes. Its small, nearly round acorns have flattened bases and slightly squared-off tips.

A rhizomatous, underground-budding plant native from southwestern Europe to western Italy and northwestern Africa. It depends entirely on fungi for nutrition; in Portugal it occurs beneath or beside woodland, pine forest and scrub, as well as on roadsides and banks.

output.summary: An underground-budding plant of unstated native origin. In Portugal it grows in meadows and pastures that are temporarily wet, on varied ground but especially sandy soils.
A perennial or rhizomatous underground-budding plant native to southwestern and east-central Europe. It grows primarily in the temperate biome.
A tree native from New South Wales to Victoria in Australia, growing primarily in the subtropical biome.
An annual native from southern Europe through Afghanistan and across Africa, growing primarily in the subtropical biome.
A bromeliad endemic to Brazil. It grows either on other plants or on rocks.
An annual herb recorded from Santa Maria, Madeira, the Desertas and Porto Santo. It is densely hairy, with broad leaves often tinged purple-red, and bears a few deep-yellow flowers.

A wet-tropical shrub or tree native from Costa Rica to western South America. It can reach 10 m tall and produces exceptionally large flower clusters, sometimes holding more than 1,000 flowers; its leaves feel rough like sandpaper.
A succulent perennial native to South Africa's Cape Province, where it grows mainly in the subtropical biome.
A temperate perennial native to the Juan Fernández Islands, Chile, Argentina and the Falkland Islands.

An epiphytic bromeliad native to Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil and Paraguay. Its long, branching stems tend to hang, while overlapping leaves are thickly covered with tiny white hairs; its short-lived white flowers usually self-pollinate.
A shrub native to the Ibero-Mauritanian region around the Iberian Peninsula and northwestern Africa. It has three-part leaves, yellow flowers that may occur in groups of three, and hairy seed pods.

A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. Features still requiring confirmation include basal leaf rosettes with long, slender runners and leaves that are nearly hairless above but densely covered with short, branched hairs beneath.
A flowering plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula. It grows in rock crevices and on limestone outcrops.
A subtropical perennial native from eastern and southeastern China to Vietnam, and from southern Kyushu in Japan to Taiwan.
An annual flowering plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula. It grows on acidic soils in fallow fields, disturbed scrub and roadsides.

A perennial herbaceous hybrid group with complex, partly uncertain ancestry. It grows from corms and bears spikes of often large, variously coloured flowers; it is widely cultivated for borders and cut flowers.
A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. It grows on acidic soils along scrub and woodland edges, paths and meadows, often near waterways where the surface is temporarily moist.

A flowering plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula. It inhabits sparse meadows in scrub clearings and beneath evergreen woods or pines; reported but unconfirmed traits include a slender stem and flattened flower clusters with fewer than ten upward-pointing rays.
A succulent subshrub native to the Mediterranean. It grows in rock cracks, sand and uncultivated ground, without a stated preference for substrate.
A plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula. It inhabits very dry rocky places and sands on granite or schist.
A flowering plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula. It grows in sparse meadows, pastures and open scrub clearings on rocky limestone or dolomite ground.
A rare plant recorded at several sites in Kabylie, Algeria, including Oued Elli Ankou at 600 metres.
An annual plant native from the western Mediterranean to central Italy. It grows around pond margins and in other wet places with moist soils.
A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. It grows on coastal dunes and sandy deposits in the floodplains of large rivers.
A flowering plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula, Ulex micranthus grows in scrub on acidic ground. It is much more common on schist than granite.
An annual grass native to mainland Portugal, Trisetaria panicea occurs in fallow land, meadows, cultivated fields, waste ground, roadsides and walls.

A perennial herb of unspecified native origin, the cut-leaved dandelion has lobed leaves with usually sickle-shaped, toothed side lobes. It bears pale-yellow flowers and reddish-brown fruits, and in Germany grows in dry grassland, sheep pasture, vineyards and along roads.
A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal, Taraxacum sundbergii is a dandelion for which no habitat information is supplied.

A flowering plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula, Euphorbia oxyphylla inhabits scrub clearings, open woodland, roadsides and banks on disturbed or stony acidic soils. Its latex is particularly toxic.
An annual flowering plant native to mainland Portugal, Tuberaria plantaginea grows in pastures, annual meadows, waste ground and scrub clearings. It favours acidic, especially sandy, soils.
An annual grass endemic to the Iberian Peninsula, Periballia involucrata grows in sparse mountain grasslands on acidic ground.

A grass endemic to the Iberian Peninsula, Anthoxanthum amarum is chiefly a woodland plant of cool sites near water, including deciduous woods, scrub and moisture-loving meadows. It is centred in the peninsula's northwest, with an isolated eastern population.

An annual native to the western Mediterranean, Filago carpetana is densely covered with greyish hairs and ends each stem in a compact flower-head cluster. It occurs in woodland clearings, roadsides, fallow fields, grazed ground and disturbed places, especially on granite or sandy siliceous soils.
A plant native from Colombia to Ecuador, Aristeguietia lamiifolia is documented as a medicine for unspecified disorders.

A perennial flowering herb endemic to the Iberian Peninsula, it grows mainly in shady woodland habitats on deep, acidic soils. Its long, soft leaves and uniformly dark-brown bracts help distinguish it from the similar Asphodelus ramosus.
A plant native to Gran Canaria in the Canary Islands, it grows mainly in the subtropical biome.
A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal, it inhabits dry, open meadows, pastures, cultivated ground, olive groves and extensively managed orchards.
A shrub native to Porto Santo in Madeira, it grows mainly in the subtropical biome.
A perennial plant native to Macaronesia and the western Mediterranean, it grows mainly in the subtropical biome.

A flowering plant endemic to central mainland Portugal, it grows in grasslands, roadsides, fields, scrub clearings and rocky crevices on silica-rich ground. Its present distribution and population size remain poorly known because it is often confused with similar plants.
A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal, it is associated with sandy coastal scrub. It grows on stabilized dunes and coastal cliffs, only rarely beneath pine or cork-oak woodland.

A flowering plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula, it grows in dry scrub and open pine or cork-oak woodland. It favours acidic sand on coastal dunes and cliffs but also occurs on sandy deposits inland.
An artificial plant hybrid with no native origin stated, Clivia × cyrtanthiflora is a cross between Clivia miniata and Clivia nobilis.

A woody-stemmed flowering plant native to the Iberian Peninsula, it grows mainly on inland, sandy acidic soils in uncultivated ground, slopes and rainfed crops. Its upright stems branch strongly from the base and bear rigid, angular branches. The plant is reported as toxic to humans and ruminants.

output.summary: An Iberian-endemic shrub with a narrow form, slightly drooping branches and brown bark that peels in thin layers. Its needle-like leaves usually grow in threes, while its cones ripen over two years from yellowish to red or copper-red.

A rhizomatous plant native to the Mediterranean, forming tussocks with clearly branched, tall stems. It is associated mainly with riverbanks and the backs of beaches, but also occurs in disturbed places.

An annual plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula. Possible identifying features, still needing confirmation, include basal fruits with no bristles or short unequal ones, and leaves whose terminal segment is much longer than the few side segments.

An annual flowering plant native to mainland Portugal and Madeira. It occurs in scrub clearings, meadows, annual pastures and cultivated fields, mainly on limestone; its capsule reportedly has conspicuous thick ridges, though this feature needs confirmation.

An annual flowering plant native to mainland Portugal and introduced in the Azores. It favours damp or shady coastal sites, often on sandy ground that floods periodically or beside ponds; its leaf stalks may be tendril-like, though this feature needs confirmation.

A low-growing perennial with two varieties documented as native to mainland Portugal. It grows in scrub clearings and pastures on disturbed acidic ground; var. latifolia may also occur on dunes and coastal rocks.

An annual flowering plant represented in mainland Portugal by two native subspecies. Both occur in dry annual grasslands in fallow land, rain-fed orchards and roadsides, particularly on basic, somewhat nitrogen-rich ground, and may be parasitized by Cuscuta planiflora.
An annual flowering plant native to mainland Portugal and Madeira. It grows in annual meadows and pastures, including fallow and agricultural fields, waste ground and scrub clearings.

A biennial or perennial herb native from Europe to Iran. It has upright, strongly ribbed stems that branch near the top, hairy divided leaves, and flower heads that may have ray florets or be entirely disc-like. It favours slopes, roadsides and deciduous woodland edges, especially on sandy, siliceous soils.
A plant with a reported range in tropical Asia, widely distributed in Myanmar. Reported medicinal uses include the whole plant as an antidote for snake poison and the leaves for intermittent fever.
A tuber-growing flowering plant native to the Mediterranean. It grows mainly in subtropical regions.
A fully parasitic flowering plant native from southern Portugal and southeastern France through Sicily and Türkiye, and in northwestern Africa. It grows mainly in subtropical regions.
A red alga whose native origin is not stated. Large strandings periodically occur on the Normandy and Brittany coasts of France.
A commercially valuable red alga whose native origin is not stated. Its firm, cartilage-like branches lie in one plane, and it inhabits wave-battered rocky shores. It is an important source of agar.
A subshrub or shrub native from the eastern United States to eastern Mexico. It grows mainly in subtropical regions.
A flowering plant endemic to southern Brazil.
A flowering plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula. In Portugal it grows on shaded, acidic ground in woodland clearings, beside granite walls and paths, and in traditional olive groves.
A tuber-growing plant hybrid native to the Mediterranean. It is a cross between Ophrys bombyliflora and Ophrys tenthredinifera.

A perennial flowering herb native from eastern Europe to the Russian Far East and northern China. It has slender spreading underground stems and conspicuously hairy upright stems. Its ray flowers are usually pink or purplish red, but rarely become white.
A bulb-forming plant native from Brazil to northeastern Argentina. It grows mainly in seasonally dry tropical regions.

A parasitic plant growing from underground buds; its native origin is not supplied. It occurs across Europe and North Africa and, in Portugal, is confined mainly to northern coastal dunes. It parasitizes Artemisia species.

A plant growing from underground buds; its native origin is not supplied. In Portugal it inhabits scrub, pinewoods and woodland, usually on limestone soils, and parasitizes rosemary and probably other shrubs.
A parasitic plant native only to the Iberian Peninsula. It grows in scrub and parasitizes rosemary.

A perennial parasitic plant; its native origin is not supplied. In Portugal it grows in hedges and fallow ground on limestone soils, parasitizing fennel or other perennial members of the carrot family. It is currently known there from only two small population centres, around Lisbon and in the Algarve.

A herbaceous parasitic plant native to the Mediterranean region. It mainly parasitizes members of the legume, daisy and mint families, and bears dense clusters of strongly curved, pale blue-violet flowers.

A parasitic broomrape native to Eurasia and North Africa. It has many slender yellowish stems but no leaves or chlorophyll, drawing nutrients from other plants’ roots. Its tubular flowers are white and blue to purple.
A shrub or low-growing shrub native from southern Ecuador to northern and central Peru. It grows mainly in subtropical regions.
A flowering plant native to the Canary Islands.
An annual flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. It grows along scrub edges, in hedges, olive groves and fallow fields, favouring cool sites with alkaline soils.

A perennial flowering herb native to the western Mediterranean, including Portugal, Spain, Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia. It grows in dry open scrub and coastal pinewoods, chiefly on acidic sandy or schist soils.

An annual herb endemic to the southwestern Iberian Peninsula. It grows near the coast in open scrub, pinewoods and annual grasslands on dry, nutrient-poor sandy soils, and is classed as Vulnerable in mainland Portugal.

A perennial flowering herb endemic to the Iberian Peninsula. It inhabits scrub clearings and rocky outcrops on basic rocks and green schist, sometimes in flood beds or places that become temporarily waterlogged; its Portuguese population is endangered and severely fragmented.

A low-growing perennial plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula. It occurs in mountain scrub clearings on acidic ground, often where Pyrenean oak woods have been degraded; in Portugal it is frequent and abundant within its small northern range.

An annual flowering plant whose native origin is not supplied. In Portugal it is known only from traditional dry-farmed olive groves on basic soils, and bears flowers consistently in threes at each node, with a central male flower between two female flowers.
An annual flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. It grows in cultivated meadows and occasionally in walls or rock cavities, favouring dry, stony, disturbed soils rich in bases.
A geophyte whose native origin is not supplied. In Portugal it is recorded as a parasite of Carlina hispanica, while its habitat remains undocumented.

A subshrub native from southern France and southern Portugal to southwestern Spain. It grows around upper saltmarsh edges and on coastal sands, with some inland populations on slightly salty clay; in mainland Portugal it is endangered and known only from the Algarve coast.

A subshrub of unspecified native origin, distributed around Mediterranean coasts. Its leafless, prostrate or rising stems carry dense clusters of small lilac flowers, and it grows in coastal salt marshes, salt steppes, cliffs and rocks.
A subshrub native to eastern Spain, growing primarily in the temperate biome.

A perennial, densely branched subshrub found on Lanzarote; its native origin is not explicitly stated. It forms fairly flat rosettes of bluish green leaves, often reddish near the tip, and bears domed clusters of pink-marked whitish flowers.
A tropical plant native to southeastern and southern Brazil. It grows on other plants or rocks, mainly in wet tropical environments.
An annual or biennial flowering plant native to the western Mediterranean. It grows mainly in subtropical environments.

A basil species native to Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda, Sudan and Ethiopia, commonly called camphor basil. Its aerial tissues have distinct chemical profiles; flowers yielded the most putative metabolites in one analysis and stems the fewest.

A perennial plant of unstated native origin, distributed across northwestern Africa, southern Europe and western Asia. It has closely grouped lower leaves, white flowers in umbrella-like clusters and small, nearly spherical fruits.

A perennial grass of unstated native origin, occurring from Hungary and the Mediterranean region to Iran. It spreads by a creeping underground stem and has rolled, threadlike grey-green leaves, with sparse flower clusters bearing straight, rough bristles.
An annual grass native to mainland Portugal and introduced to Madeira. In Portugal it grows in meadows, fallow ground and annual pastures on dry or seasonally wet soils, avoiding lime-rich ground.
A plant species of unspecified type and native origin. It has been recorded in ravine bottoms, Stora and several Kabylie localities, where it was described as rare.
Bulbous plant native to southwestern Europe. It grows in sunny mountain meadows and woodland clearings, often on stony ground.

Low-growing flowering plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula. It inhabits dry, stony openings in scrub, unused ground and pastures; reported traits needing confirmation include leaves in threes and generally flexible stem hairs.
Perennial plant native from the Russian Far East through northern China and Korea to central and southern Japan. It grows mainly in temperate regions.
Perennial flowering plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula. It occurs in pastures and along woodland edges.
Perennial plant native to Spain. Its leaflets are deeply divided and narrowed at the base.

Perennial plant endemic to mainland Portugal. It grows in dry meadows and openings in scrub or woodland on limestone soils, and has threadlike green leaves with rolled margins. Its small known range and declining habitat contributed to its Vulnerable assessment in mainland Portugal.
Annual plant of unstated native origin. In Portugal it occurs in dry meadows, fallow fields, pastures and roadsides.
Cactus native to the deserts of Mexico. Its solitary rounded or slightly cylindrical body bears exceptionally numerous thin, wavy ribs, white spines and white-to-purple flowers.

Cactus tribe of unstated native origin, distributed from North America to northeastern South America. Its members form shrubs or cushions with strongly jointed, cylindrical shoots; most have only short-lived leaf remnants, though Pereskiopsis and Quiabentia retain succulent leaves.

Quillwort of unstated native origin, documented near Belalcázar and at Sierra Morena in Spain. One collection grew on temporarily flooded granitic ground, while several others came from streamside localities.
A plant with underground storage organs, endemic to the Iberian Peninsula. It grows in sparse coastal grassland on consolidated dunes or sandy soils.
A plant species of unspecified native origin, recorded from several northern Algerian localities and described as rare.
A flowering plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula. It grows in grassland, pasture and scrub clearings on acidic, stony or sandy soils derived from schist or sandstone.

An annual herb native to mainland Portugal and distributed across much of the Mediterranean region. It has solitary blue flowers with pale tubes and distinctly triangular lobes, and grows in dry, clay-rich pastures, field margins and roadsides.
A plant subgenus of unspecified native origin, found from Bhutan and Bangladesh south through Myanmar, Thailand, Laos and Vietnam to western China.
A plant subgenus of unspecified native origin, found in Southeast Asia in Indonesia and Malaysia.
A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. It grows in wet mountain grassland and sparse grassland that floods temporarily, over rock, sand or gravel.
An annual plant of unspecified native origin, recorded in Europe. It favors dry annual grassland, pasture, uncultivated ground, and clearings in scrub or pine woods, without a strong soil preference.
A succulent annual native from east-central Europe through the Mediterranean region to northern Iran. It grows mainly in temperate environments.

A moss of unspecified native origin, found only in Europe. It forms small cushions, usually on deciduous bark near water, and is recognizable by strongly curled dry leaves, a transparent bordered leaf base and hairy bell-shaped caps over its capsules.
An annual flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. It grows in annual grasslands within scrub clearings and dry orchards, favouring somewhat disturbed, mainly basic soils.
A subshrub native to southeastern and southern Brazil. It grows mainly in seasonally dry tropical regions.

An annual or perennial herb found on disturbed saline ground and around saltmarsh scrub in Portugal. In mainland Portugal it is endangered and known only from three locations on the southern Algarve coast, although the assessment is based on limited information.
A tuberous hybrid plant native to the western Mediterranean. It is the cross Ophrys bombyliflora × Ophrys speculum and grows mainly in subtropical regions.

An annual herb with a strong smell, deeply toothed triangular leaves and a pyramidal flower cluster. It occurs across Europe, India and temperate Asia to China, typically on nutrient-rich soils in fields, gardens and waste ground.
A plant native from Bolivia through southern Brazil and other parts of southern South America.
A low-growing flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. It inhabits dry scrub and clearings in cork oak, oak and holm oak woodland on varied substrates.
A low-growing plant found on coastal sands in Portugal, especially primary and secondary dunes.
An annual plant found near the Portuguese coast on sandy soils. It grows in annual grasslands on stable dunes, sandy-scrub clearings, forest firebreaks and pinewood margins.
An annual or perennial herb found on sandy ground in Portugal. Its subspecies occupy habitats ranging from coastal dunes and dry scrub clearings to inland sands, stony places and river deposits.

Flowering plant native to Macaronesia and the Mediterranean basin. In Corsica it is considered rare and may be overlooked because flowering is sporadic, its colouring is inconspicuous and it often occupies disturbed ground.
Annual plant native to the western Mediterranean, growing mainly in subtropical regions.
Flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. It favours sandy soils in uncultivated fields, field margins, roadsides and coastal sands, although its Portuguese distribution remains uncertain.
Tree native from Peru through Brazil to northwestern Argentina. It grows mainly in seasonally dry tropical regions and is used medicinally.
Plant species with no native origin or growth form stated, documented from many localities across Algeria and described as common.
Moss of unstated native origin, restricted to temperate parts of the Northern Hemisphere. It forms soft, loose, velvety mats ranging from yellow-green to brown and especially favours shaded places.

Moss of unstated native origin, occurring in Europe, western Asia, Madeira, the Canary Islands and Algeria. Fresh plants smell of cucumber when crushed; other useful identifiers are their hollow, spoon-shaped leaves and unusually strong central leaf rib.
Moss of unstated native origin. It is excluded from Algeria because the sole reported specimen there was later identified as another species.
Genus of flowering plants native from the Mediterranean, North Africa and Chad to southern Africa, Arabia and Iran. It belongs to the mint family and includes 13 accepted species.
Shrub or tree native from peninsular Thailand to Malesia, growing mainly in wet tropical regions. Its roots and leaves have medicinal uses, but the leaves are reported poisonous.

output.summary: A perennial or subshrub native from central and southern Portugal into Spain, growing mainly in the temperate biome.
A flowering plant native to the Canary Islands and from southwestern Europe to North Africa, growing mainly in the subtropical biome.

A herbaceous plant native to the Mediterranean region. Its small, hairy leaves cover stems that lie along the ground, and its inconspicuous flowers and overall grey colour can make it easy to overlook.
A flowering plant native to Cape Verde and considered endangered. Its crushed, heated leaves are traditionally applied externally to inflammation.

A section of plants native to New Zealand, Rapa, the Falkland Islands and South America, with almost all its species occurring in New Zealand. Members range from dwarf shrubs to small trees and have leaves arranged in four perpendicular rows; alpine forms may have leaves reduced to thick scales.
A shrub hybrid native to New Zealand’s South Island, growing mainly in the temperate biome. It is a cross between Veronica speciosa and Veronica stricta.
A perennial, rhizome-forming grass native to the Canary Islands and from Europe to the Mediterranean, growing mainly in the temperate biome.
An annual, partly parasitic herb native to the western Mediterranean. It grows upright with many branches and is densely covered in sticky, glandular hairs; its flowers are usually pale yellow.
An artificial plant hybrid of unstated origin, produced from Hypericum addingtonii, H. calycinum and H. hookerianum.
An aquatic flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. It inhabits cold, shallow, nutrient-poor rivers and smaller streams with neutral or acidic water.
A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. It grows on disturbed, trampled ground beside paths, especially on limestone or dolomite soils.

A spiny, much-branched shrub endemic to the southern Iberian Peninsula, from Portugal to Jaén. Its stems end in spines and its flowers occur singly or in pairs; it inhabits heath and scrub on thin soils over slate or granite.

A low woody flowering plant whose listed varieties, var. gracilis and var. ramosissima, are native to mainland Portugal. It chiefly grows in sandy scrub on coastal dunes and cliffs, occurring more rarely in abandoned dry orchards or river alluvium.
A perennial plant native from Bolivia through southern Brazil to northern Argentina. It grows mainly in subtropical environments.

A filamentous green alga with no native origin stated; it occurs worldwide and is typical of soil communities. It is common on cultivated soils, often dominating them, and its cylindrical cells become barrel-shaped over time.
An herbaceous grass from the Mediterranean region. It grows in annual grasslands, wasteland and scrub on sandy or limestone ground.

A unicellular alga with no native origin stated, recorded in European waters. Its nearly round cell has a central constriction forming two halves, each with one round chloroplast; it usually inhabits neutral, moderately nutrient-rich peat cuttings, bogs, ditches and ponds, but can tolerate slightly alkaline water.
A plant native from the Iberian Peninsula to Morocco. It grows mainly in the temperate biome.

A non-spiny evergreen shrub endemic to the central and western Iberian Peninsula, including northern Portugal. Its upright green-grey branches bear yellow flowers in spring and early summer, and it forms large stands on sunny mountain slopes with granite or quartzite soils.
A herbaceous fern endemic to the Azores, it grows in plantations, ravines, mountain slopes and laurel forests. Invasive plants compete with it and alter its habitat.
A red alga of unstated native origin, it is recorded from the Mediterranean, Atlantic, English Channel and North Sea.
A flowering plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula, it occurs in mainland Portugal.

A rough-haired perennial herb of unstated native origin, it occurs in northern Iberia and French Cerdanya; southeastern Swedish populations may not be native. It grows in pastures, meadows, stream margins and roadsides, bearing yellow flowers and numerous hairy fruits.
A perennial grass hybrid native to the Azores, it grows mainly in temperate conditions. It is the cross Holcus lanatus × Holcus rigidus.
An annual grass endemic to Santa Maria in the Azores, it forms dense tufts. Its leaves are thickly hairy on both sides, and its oblong flower clusters contain compact spikelets.

A perennial herb or small shrub native to western and southwestern Europe, it is associated with temperate regions. Mainland plants have pink flowers and occupy coastal dunes, scrub and rocks, as well as wet inland meadows, hedges and banks.

An emerald-green moss of unstated native origin, it grows on sunny, lime-poor ground that is moderately moist or dry. Its nearly upright capsule has a densely felted cap, and its spores mature in winter.

A perennial herb of unstated native origin, it is found in the Iberian Peninsula and North Africa. It has an underground tuber and grows mainly in sandy pastures, cork-oak woods, holm-oak woods and pine woods.

A perennial flowering plant endemic to the western Iberian Peninsula, it is very rare and occurs in western Portugal and Galicia. It grows in warm, very wet or seasonally flooded vegetation and has deeply grooved fruit with prominent finger-like warts.
An annual native to the Iberian Peninsula, growing mainly in the temperate biome.
A grass native to the western Mediterranean, including southwestern Europe and northwestern Africa. In Portugal it inhabits dry, sandy meadows and clearings.
An evergreen flowering plant native to the Caribbean and cultivated as an ornamental. It has fleshy shoots, rounded light-green leaves and inconspicuous flowers packed into long, dense spikes.

A perennial fern native to Macaronesia and Cádiz in Spain. It has short, fleshy creeping stems and triangular, deeply lobed fronds that emerge in autumn. It closely resembles Polypodium cambricum and may require microscopic examination to distinguish.
An annual flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. There it grows in scrub clearings, woodland edges and perennial grassland, generally on limestone soils.

A perennial herb with no stated native origin, found across much of northern Iberia and the western French Pyrenees. It has a rounded underground tuber and white flowers, and occurs chiefly beneath oak, beech and pine woodland, but also in meadows, clearings and rocky ground.

A freshwater red alga with no stated native origin, recorded in Europe, China and North America. It forms dense blackish-purple tufts of mostly unbranched, hollow threads and grows on submerged stones and wood in clean, cold headwater streams.

An evergreen thorny shrub native from the Mediterranean basin eastward to the Arabian Peninsula and Iran. Its tangled branches commonly become spines, while its tough leaves vary greatly in shape from rounded to narrow and needle-like.
A flowering plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula. In Portugal it grows in dry meadows, pastures, scrub clearings and pine woods, especially on coastal sandy soils.
An annual flowering plant native to mainland Portugal, it grows in sandy meadows, generally near the coast.
A flowering plant with no native origin supplied, it grows in openings among salt-tolerant scrub in Portuguese estuaries and salt marshes. It favours sandy, salty soils.

A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal, it inhabits dry, rocky or somewhat disturbed places around woodlands, scrub, banks and fallow ground. It is the only known host of the parasitic plant Orobanche nepetae.

An annual herb endemic to the Iberian Peninsula and North Africa, it grows in fairly shaded scrub on slopes. Its branching stems bear tendrils, pink flowers and two contrasting fruit forms: lower one-seeded fruits and upper two-seeded fruits, often with hooked tips.

An evergreen tree native to Macaronesia and endemic to the Canary Islands and Madeira, it is part of laurel forest. It has glossy dark-green oval leaves, often bearing mite-induced galls, and elongated fruits that become blackish when ripe.
A plant with no native origin supplied, it has been recorded frequently across several parts of Algeria, including Tlemcen, Algiers, Tiaret, Aurès and Kabylie.
A flowering grass endemic to the Iberian Peninsula; no habitat information is supplied.
A perennial native from Brazil to northeastern Argentina, it grows primarily in subtropical environments.

An annual flowering plant native to mainland Portugal, it grows in farm-associated or nutrient-rich meadows. Possible identifying features, still requiring confirmation, include flower clusters with only two rays and highly divided upper leaves.

A deciduous shrub with no native origin supplied, it occurs on Madeira and the Canary Islands. Its yellow flowers have a strongly sweet fragrance and are picked shortly after opening for fresh extraction of essential oil used in perfumery.
A temperate shrub native to southeastern China, South Korea, central and southern Japan, and the Nansei Islands.
A wet-tropical tree native from western tropical Africa east to Zambia.

A perennial subshrub native from the western Mediterranean through North Africa to the central Sahara. It has a woody base, conspicuously hairy stems and leaves, and reddish-purple flowers striped with white.
An annual flowering plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula. In Portugal it grows in sandy soil with temporary moisture beside paths and in meadows and pastures.
A perennial plant of unstated native origin. In Portugal it grows in rock crevices, especially in siliceous rock, and its fresh leaves release a subtle characteristic smell when rubbed.

An ecologically diverse species complex of unstated native origin, with wild tetraploid plants widely distributed around the Mediterranean. It gave rise to cultivated forms including the robust-stemmed common leek and slender-leaved kurrat, which remain fully interfertile with the wild plants.

An annual or winter-annual herb of unstated native origin. Its branched, creeping-to-rising stems have a single line of hairs between each pair of leaves, while its flowers have deeply split petals and usually three to five purple-violet anthers.

A small annual herb of unstated native origin. In mainland Portugal it is known only from tiny, scattered populations on the southern slope of Serra de Ficalho, chiefly in open abandoned olive groves on dry, sunny limestone soil, and is assessed there as Vulnerable.
A flowering plant native to Central and Southern Europe.

An annual grass native from western Europe through the Mediterranean to the western Himalayas. It has narrow, pointed leaves and a straight, one-sided flower spike with closely pressed, bristle-tipped flowers.

A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal and restricted globally to the Iberian Peninsula and northwestern Africa. In Portugal it grows in rocky grasslands on basic soils and is known only from three populations in the Upper Douro basin, though its current distribution is uncertain.

An annual plant native from southeastern Portugal into Spain and endemic to the southwestern Iberian Peninsula. It grows in dry, rocky grasslands and slopes derived from schist, with its flower clusters spread along the flowering stem rather than concentrated at the tip.
A shrub or tree hybrid native to the Iberian Peninsula. It is a cross between Quercus faginea and Quercus rotundifolia and grows mainly in temperate regions.

A tree-like cactus occurring across several states of Mexico. Its upright, usually unbranched columnar stems have four to seven broad ribs, while reddish funnel-shaped flowers develop near the stem tips among dense bristles.
A subshrub native from southern Siberia to northern China. It grows mainly in temperate regions.
A moss recorded widely across Algeria, from beaches at sea level to mountain sites. It is described as very common there.
A moss recorded frequently in northern Algeria. It was also found in the colon of the Tyrolean Iceman.
A moss native to the Northern Hemisphere. Its leaves range from yellow to a coppery yellow, and it has been recorded frequently in Algeria.
A moss recorded across many parts of Algeria, from coastal beaches and dunes to mountain locations. It is described as very common there.

A moss found across western North America, Europe, North Africa and western Asia, especially in coastal temperate rainforests near sea level. It usually grows on tree trunks and branches, and its slender leaves are often dusted with distinctive brown reproductive fragments.
A temperate subshrub native from southwestern Siberia to western Mongolia.
A flowering plant native to Borneo, specifically Sabah and Sarawak. It grows on other plants, mainly in wet tropical habitats.
A tree native to southeastern Brazil, from Rio de Janeiro to Minas Gerais. It grows mainly in wet tropical habitats.
A moss recorded frequently at numerous Algerian localities, including Kabylie, Algiers, Oran and El-Kala National Park.

A plant with a Mediterranean-Atlantic distribution across Europe and North Africa. In Tunisia it was found on mud deposited around large roots in a swampy willow grove. Its reddish-brown spores occur in distinctive groups of four.

A moss found in boreal regions and the Pacific Northwest, where it can dominate moderately rich forest habitats. Its fuzzy, tail-like appearance inspires the name “electrified cat’s tail moss,” and it usually grows on humus-rich ground in mountain forests.
A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. It grows in meadows and pastures on poor, stony or sandy, acidic and somewhat moist soils.

A flowering plant endemic to northwestern Iberia, from northwestern Portugal to southern Galicia. It inhabits mountain vegetation along runoff channels and other damp places, usually over granite. In mainland Portugal it is assessed as Near Threatened.

A flowering plant sparsely distributed from southern France to the Algarve. It occurs only in seasonally waterlogged places with limestone, clay or marl soils, including temporary ponds. It is globally threatened and assessed as Critically Endangered in mainland Portugal, where only one location is known.
A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. It grows in scrub clearings on coastal sands and readily hybridizes with Tuberaria guttata.

A flowering plant whose two listed subspecies are endemic to the Iberian Peninsula. In mountain areas, subsp. humilis inhabits granite crevices, while subsp. odorata grows in sparse grassland on sandy, granite-derived soils.
A leafy moss of unspecified native origin. It is reproducing in Sweden.
A shrub or subshrub native to the Mediterranean region. It grows mainly in subtropical environments.
A shrub of unspecified native origin, found in the Maghreb and southern Spain. It is generally under one metre tall and is used in the Maghreb to construct sheepfolds.
A moss of unspecified native origin. It has been recorded widely across Algeria, from dunes and forests to mountain localities, and the account describes it as common.
A flowering plant of unspecified native origin. It is distributed across Sweden, Denmark, Germany, Switzerland, Austria and Italy.
An annual flowering plant of unspecified native origin. In Portugal it grows in sunny, dry pastures and grasslands with annual vegetation, on siliceous, sandy soils.

A shrub or subshrub native to the western and central Mediterranean Basin, from Portugal and Spain east to Italy and south into northwestern Africa. An early account places it in coastal parts of Portugal.
A shrub native from southern India to southern Indochina. It grows mainly in wet tropical environments.
A tuberous hybrid native to Europe, Anacamptis × olida grows mainly in subtropical regions. It is a cross between A. coriophora and A. morio.
A plant of unspecified native origin, Sonchus microcephalus has the unusual chromosome number 2n = 30.
A perennial herb occurring in Spain and Portugal.
A flowering legume native to Eurasia and Africa, Biserrula pelecinus is the only accepted species in its genus. It is legally protected in France's Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur region.
An annual species native to the Mediterranean, Biserrula epiglottis grows mainly in subtropical regions. In Portugal, it inhabits rocky grasslands on very dry, stony, alkaline soils.
A tuberous hybrid native to southwestern Europe, Ophrys × chobautii grows mainly in subtropical regions. It is a cross between O. lutea and O. speculum.
A perennial cultigen derived from artificial hybrids, Cenchrus × cupreus grows mainly in subtropical regions. It is a cross between C. elegans and C. setaceus.
A plant native to southeastern Brazil, Aechmea coelestis occurs from Espírito Santo to Santa Catarina.
A scrambling annual native from southern Europe to the Aegean Islands, Lathyrus articulatus grows mainly in temperate regions.
A shrub or tree native to China, Fontanesia fortunei grows mainly in temperate regions.
A tuber-forming hybrid plant native to southern Europe, chiefly in temperate environments. Its parent species are Ophrys apifera and Ophrys tenthredinifera.
A temperate plant species native to Madeira.
An annual plant native from southwestern Germany to southwestern Europe, chiefly in subtropical environments.

A deciduous tree with conflicting native-range accounts in the supplied sources. Its broad leaves are green above and grey-white and downy beneath, while its dull brownish-red fruit ripens in late autumn. The edible fruit was sold at open-air markets in Fontainebleau until the 1950s.

output.summary: A partly woody shrub native to the southwestern Pacific, chiefly in wet tropical environments. It is used medicinally.
A plant species whose native origin is not specified; it is widely distributed from Egypt to South Africa and across the Arabian Peninsula, Maldives and Sri Lanka.
A plant species whose native origin is not specified, recorded in the forests of La Calle and described as very rare.

An aquatic moss with no native origin specified, normally found on rocks in fast-flowing streams in open or wooded areas. Its green to brownish stems have few branches, and overlapping concave leaves give them a cylindrical appearance.
A hybrid tree native to the Iberian Peninsula, chiefly in temperate environments. Its parent species are Quercus lusitanica and Quercus orocantabrica.
A tuber-forming hybrid plant native to the western Mediterranean, chiefly in subtropical environments. Its parent species are Ophrys scolopax and Ophrys tenthredinifera.

A herb of unspecified native origin, found in Portugal in coastal grasslands, fallow ground, roadsides and soils derived from limestone or other basic rocks. It was first detected in Portugal in August 2023.

A succulent subshrub native from Cameroon and Eritrea through eastern and central Africa and the Arabian Peninsula to the Indian Subcontinent and Tibet. It primarily inhabits seasonally dry tropical regions.
A flowering plant endemic to the Mediterranean, including parts of southern Europe, North Africa and Turkey. Its flower segments lack spots but carry a narrow green or pink stripe.
A succulent hybrid subshrub native to Madeira. It is the natural hybrid of Aeonium glandulosum and Aeonium glutinosum and primarily grows in the subtropical biome.

A flowering plant endemic to the northwestern Iberian Peninsula, including mainland Portugal. It remains poorly known, and available information is insufficient to assess its extinction risk in Portugal.

A bark-growing epiphyte of unspecified native origin, recorded in Mediterranean and Macaronesian Europe and North Africa. It usually occupies open woodland or isolated trees and has an immersed capsule topped by a covering with a tuft of robust upright hairs.
A perennial native to Portugal and endemic to Baixo Alentejo. It grows in wet places beside lagoons and temporary pools, and in damp pasture on sandy soils.
An artificial plant hybrid of unspecified geographic origin, produced by crossing Hylotelephium spectabile with Hylotelephium telephium subsp. maximum.
An annual native to the western Mediterranean. In Portugal it occurs in fallow and cultivated fields, open scrub and woodland, meadows and annual pastures.
An annual herb found in Portugal in fallow ground, cork-oak woodlands, clearings and cultivated fields. It grows mainly on sandy, acidic soils.
A herbaceous geophyte recorded in Portugal, where it grows in moist, semi-deciduous oak woods on north-facing slopes with schist soils. Its leaves resemble those of Thalictrum.
An annual flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. It occurs in pastures, scrub clearings, farmland and roadsides, preferring alkaline ground that is sometimes disturbed.
A tuberous hybrid native to southern Europe. It grows mainly in subtropical regions and has Ophrys bombyliflora and O. scolopax as its parent species.
An annual native to the Canary Islands, western Europe, the Mediterranean through Central Asia, and the western Himalayas. It grows mainly in temperate regions.
An annual grass found in Portuguese coastal dunes, sandy grasslands and pinewoods. It is self-supporting and has simple, broad leaves.

An annual plant found in Portugal in dry grasslands, pastures, fallow ground and waste places, usually on sandy, nitrogen-enriched soils. Its flower cluster stands clearly above the upper leaf sheath, while its ovary and fruit are hairless.
An annual plant.
A tuberous orchid hybrid native from Europe to the Caucasus. It grows mainly in temperate regions and has Orchis mascula and O. provincialis as its parent species.
A shrub hybrid native to the western Mediterranean, it grows mainly in subtropical areas. Its parents are Cistus populifolius and Cistus salviifolius.

A flowering plant endemic to northeastern mainland Portugal, it is restricted to the Bragança–Vinhais massif. It grows in cracks in ultrabasic serpentinite rocks and in dry grasslands on ultrabasic soils. Fewer than 2,500 mature plants were estimated, and it is considered Near Threatened in mainland Portugal.

A grass native to the western Mediterranean region, it inhabits sunny, dry places, especially on limestone. In Portugal it is known only from one population on maritime slopes in the Serra da Arrábida, where it usually grows in limestone rock cracks.
A flowering plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula, it grows in scrub clearings, on banks and beside paths. It tolerates acidic or basic, shallow soils that are somewhat enriched with nutrients.
A flowering plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula, it grows in heathland and disturbed uncultivated ground at mountain and subalpine elevations. It is associated with siliceous substrates.
A plant species native from southern France to the Iberian Peninsula.

A perennial of unspecified native origin, it has solitary, stout stems with narrow, folded leaves concentrated near the base. Its flower rays are yellow, sometimes purplish outside, and its fruits bear dirty-white feathery hairs.
A flowering plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula, it grows in sandy places near the coast. It occurs on secondary dunes, often among coastal scrub, juniper and pine woodland.
A flowering sedge native to the Azores, it grows from underground stems and occurs mainly in the temperate biome.
A shrub hybrid native to the Mediterranean region, it grows mainly in subtropical areas. Its parents are Cistus monspeliensis and Cistus salviifolius.
A shrub hybrid native to the western Mediterranean, Cistus × stenophyllus is a cross between C. ladanifer and C. monspeliensis.
A tuberous plant native from southwestern France to northwestern Africa. It grows mainly in subtropical regions.

A tuft-forming grass native to the Old World, Arrhenatherum longifolium grows through winter and spring. Its stiff blue-green leaves are briefly hairy and roll up in drought; greenish-white, sometimes violet flowers appear from May to July.
A tuberous hybrid native from Europe to the eastern Mediterranean, Anacamptis × simorrensis is a cross between A. coriophora and A. pyramidalis. It grows mainly in temperate regions.
A bulbous plant native to southeastern France, central and southern Spain, and west-central Portugal. In Portugal it grows in scrub clearings on siliceous soils.
A perennial flowering plant native to the western and southern Mediterranean. It inhabits rocky places and has a basal leaf rosette with solitary blue or purple flower heads that bloom in spring.

A perennial herb native to Portugal and endemic to its western and southwestern coasts. It grows in coastal limestone scrub and fixed marine sands, bearing solitary terminal flower heads with purple or bright-pink outer florets.

A nightshade subgenus distributed across tropical and subtropical regions worldwide, with a few species in temperate areas. Its roughly 350–450 species commonly bear spines and star-shaped hairs on their vegetative parts.

An annual plant native from Europe to Siberia and the Caucasus. It has slender spreading branches, finely divided leaves and bright-blue, long-spurred flowers that open from April to July.
An annual flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. It grows in sandy soil near the coast, particularly along scrub edges and in roadside meadows.
A scrambling shrub native from the eastern Mediterranean eastward to Turkmenistan and the western Himalaya.
A bulbous plant native from northern Portugal to northwestern and north-central Spain. It grows primarily in the temperate biome.

An annual herb endemic to the southwestern Iberian Peninsula, from eastern Seville to Portugal’s Algarve and Alentejo. It grows in short-lived pastures on stony or sandy siliceous soils and has hairless blue-violet flowers with dark veins, a yellow-orange centre and a curved spur.

A perennial herb occurring across the eastern Mediterranean. Its flowers have a velvety black-violet lip, reddish-brown underside and a bright blue marking formed by two oval patches; the bee Andrena morio has been observed pollinating it.

A perennial sedge occurring in Macaronesia, northwestern Africa and Europe east to central Turkey. It forms dense clumps and has upright triangular stems; its fruiting spikes spread conspicuously, with pale-brown scales and relatively small fruit cases.
A worldwide section of Carex sedges containing about 70–90 species. Its 31 North American species commonly inhabit wetlands such as shorelines, marshes and tundra.
A flowering grass native to mainland Portugal. It grows on sandy soils in dunes and salt marshes.

A perennial woody bamboo native to China and Japan. It spreads widely through underground rhizomes, and mass flowering may be separated by more than a century. Young spring shoots are eaten cooked as a vegetable, but are bitter raw and require boiling in plenty of water with several water changes.

output.summary: A perennial herb native to the western and central Iberian Peninsula. It grows along roadsides, banks, ditches, riverbanks and woodland edges or clearings, and bears daisy-like flower heads on upright, often branched stems.
An annual native to the Mediterranean region, growing primarily in the temperate biome.

A flowering plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula, particularly its southwest and centre. It grows in meadows and shrubland clearings on acidic soils derived from sandstone or gravel. In mainland Portugal it is confined to Alto Alentejo and assessed as Vulnerable.
An annual native from Macaronesia and the Mediterranean eastwards to Iran. It grows primarily in the subtropical biome.
An annual native from southeastern Portugal through central and southern Spain to Morocco. In Portugal it grows beside roads and paths and in rain-fed fields on limestone soil.
A rhizome-forming plant native to Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. It grows primarily in the wet tropical biome.
A subshrub hybrid native to Flores in the Azores. It grows primarily in the subtropical biome and is the hybrid of Leontodon hochstetteri and Leontodon saxatilis.
Plant type and native origin are not stated in the supplied source. It is reported as rare, with records from Tiaret and the Aleppo pine forests of Bäinem and El Riath.

A flowering plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula, occurring naturally in mainland Portugal and the western coast of A Coruña in Galicia. It inhabits rock crevices, scree, rocky ground and roadsides, and also colonises cracks in urban walls. Its flower stalks are longer than the sepals, distinguishing it from the commonly cultivated Antirrhinum majus.
An aquatic subshrub hybrid native to western and southwestern Europe. It grows primarily in the temperate biome and is the hybrid of Ranunculus omiophyllus and Ranunculus tripartitus.
An artificial hybrid with no native origin stated, it is a cross between Mesembryanthemum cordifolium and M. haeckelianum.
A geophyte endemic to the Iberian Peninsula.

An aromatic subshrub native to the western Mediterranean, it has many yellow flower heads and densely hairy leaf undersides. It occurs in scrub clearings, banks and abandoned fields, generally on stony ground, and also on coastal sands.

A flowering perennial endemic to the Iberian Peninsula and native to mainland Portugal. It grows in damp tall-herb meadows, woodland clearings and heath, sometimes beside waterways or in rocky places, on siliceous soils.
A plant species native to eastern and southern Brazil, it grows mainly in seasonally dry tropical regions.

A grass native to mainland Portugal, where it grows in limestone fissures on coastal cliffs. It is known there only from Cabo Espichel to Serra da Arrábida, but is frequent locally on south-facing cliffs and stony ground.

An artificial hybrid conifer with no native origin, Leyland cypress is a cross between Nootka and Monterey cypresses. It grows rapidly into a dense, large tree widely planted for hedges and screens; it is usually sterile and propagated mainly from cuttings.
A succulent perennial native to northeastern Mexico, it grows mainly in desert or dry shrubland.

A densely grey-haired annual native to western and southern Iberia and northwestern Morocco. It grows on coastal sands, around coastal woodland and marsh edges, especially in trampled places with siliceous soils, and bears a dense terminal cluster of flower heads.
A flowering plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula.
Artificial plant hybrid of unspecified native origin, combining Canna glauca, C. indica and C. iridiflora.
Tree hybrid native to the western Mediterranean and associated primarily with subtropical regions. Its parents are Quercus canariensis and Q. faginea.
Flowering grass native to mainland Portugal. It grows in annual grasslands on acidic, sandy ground.
Flowering plant native only to the Iberian Peninsula. In Portugal, it grows beneath woodland cover and on slopes, favouring shady, cool places with acidic ground.
Perennial or rhizome-forming plant native from Portugal to southwestern Spain. It grows primarily in subtropical regions.
Perennial herb of unspecified native origin, occurring on the Iberian Peninsula.
Artificial plant hybrid of unspecified native origin, produced from Vitis labrusca and V. vinifera.

Annual to biennial herb, sometimes persisting longer, native to Madeira. Its upper stems bear star-shaped hairs and numerous glandular hairs, while its flower heads are golden yellow. It grows mainly on dry rocky soils, but also occurs in shady, humid stink-laurel forest and beside roads.
An annual or biennial herb with no native origin stated, it occurs in western Europe. In Portugal it grows on somewhat moist soils in fallow ground and along scrub margins.
An artificial hybrid genus of unspecified origin, × Graptoveria comprises crosses between Echeveria and Graptopetalum. The source lists two accepted hybrid species.

An annual herb endemic to the Algarve coast of Portugal, it has deep-yellow flowers marked by two dark reddish-brown stripes. It grows in scrub clearings on sandy, often gravelly soils and has been preliminarily assessed as Vulnerable.
A shrub or tree hybrid native to Spain, Quercus × numantina grows mainly in the temperate biome. It is a cross between Q. faginea and Q. pyrenaica.

A flowering grass native to continental Portugal, it also occurs across southern and western Europe. In Portugal it occurs in cool sites ranging from stream margins to oak woods and heathlands.
A shrub hybrid native to the western Mediterranean, Quercus × tingitana grows mainly in the subtropical biome. It is a cross between Q. faginea and Q. lusitanica.

A bulbous perennial herb endemic to the Canary Islands, where it occurs on every island. It bears basal leaves and small lilac-to-blue flowers in a loose cluster atop a stalk coloured green below, reddish-brown in the middle and lilac above.

A bulbous perennial herb native to the Canary Islands, Morocco and Western Sahara, it can reach about half a metre tall. It has long basal leaves and small, six-parted lilac flowers clustered atop a stalk; its ovary is blue.
An annual plant native to the Canary Islands, the Mediterranean and Ethiopia, it grows mainly in the subtropical biome.

A shrub or tree native to southern tropical and southern Africa, the Kei-apple is usually evergreen, drought-resistant and armed with long sharp thorns. Its yellow fruits have juicy, sour, orange-apricot-flavoured flesh and are eaten raw or cooked.

An artificial cactus hybrid created in England around the mid-1800s from two species native to southeastern Brazil. Grown as a houseplant, it commonly flowers around Christmas and has drooping branches, segments without sharp teeth and nearly symmetrical flowers.

A deciduous hybrid tree of unstated geographic origin. Its steep inner branches and whip-like drooping outer branches form a narrow, tall crown, while its yellow flowers appear relatively late, around the end of July.
A temperate perennial hybrid native to Europe, formed from Prunella grandiflora and P. laciniata.
A red alga of unstated native origin, belonging to the Bangiaceae family.

An annual native to Macaronesia, south-central and eastern Europe, the Mediterranean and the western Himalayas. In Portugal it occurs in farmland, fallow and uncultivated ground, especially dry disturbed places.

An alga of unstated native origin whose two studied varieties may ultimately prove to be separate species. The typical variety has swollen branch tips, while var. adhaerens lacks them; worldwide records of the latter remain uncertain and may represent a species complex.
A succulent hybrid subshrub native to Northern Province, formed from Kalanchoe luciae and K. sexangularis.
A leguminous shrub or tree native from Mexico to Honduras and eastern Cuba. It grows primarily in seasonally dry tropical regions.
A succulent subshrub native to southeastern Madagascar, it grows mainly in seasonally dry tropical environments.

An annual native from Macaronesia and the Mediterranean eastward to the western Himalayas, it grows mainly in temperate environments.
